question_text: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
explanation: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. It races around the Sun faster than any other planet, completing a year in just 88 Earth days.

question_text: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
explanation: Jupiter is the biggest planet. More than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it, and it is mostly made of gas.

question_text: Which planet is famous for its bright, icy rings?
explanation: Saturn's rings are made of billions of pieces of ice and rock. Other planets have rings too, but Saturn's are by far the brightest.

question_text: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
explanation: Mars looks reddish because its soil is full of rusty iron. You can sometimes spot it as a red dot in the night sky.

question_text: How many planets are in our solar system?
explanation: There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Pluto used to be counted but is now called a dwarf planet.

question_text: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
explanation: Venus is the hottest planet because thick clouds trap heat near its surface. Even though Mercury is closer to the Sun, Venus stays warmer.

question_text: Which is the farthest planet from the Sun?
explanation: Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets. It is so far away that one trip around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years.

question_text: What planet do we live on?
explanation: Our home is Earth, the third planet from the Sun. It is the only planet we know of where life lives.

question_text: Which planet spins on its side, almost like a rolling ball?
explanation: Uranus is tipped over so much that it rolls around the Sun on its side. Scientists think a giant collision long ago knocked it over.

question_text: Which planet has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot?
explanation: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a huge storm that has been swirling for hundreds of years. It is so big that Earth could fit inside it.

question_text: Which is the smallest of the eight planets?
explanation: Mercury is the smallest planet, only a little larger than our Moon. It also has no atmosphere to keep it warm at night.

question_text: What color does Neptune look from space?
explanation: Neptune looks deep blue because of a gas called methane in its atmosphere. The methane soaks up red light and reflects blue.

question_text: What goes around the Earth once each month?
explanation: The Moon takes about 27 days to circle the Earth. That is why we sometimes say a month is roughly a 'moon-th'.

question_text: What do we call it when the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun?
explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun's light from reaching part of the Earth. It can turn the daytime sky dim for a few minutes.

question_text: What do we call it when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon?
explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon. The Moon often turns a soft red color during one.

question_text: Why do we have day and night?
options: The Sun moves around the Earth
The Earth spins on its axis
explanation: The Earth spins like a top, so different parts face the Sun at different times. The side facing the Sun has day, and the other side has night.

question_text: Why does the Earth have seasons?
options: The Earth is tilted as it orbits the Sun
The Sun gets hotter and cooler
Clouds cover the Sun in winter
explanation: The Earth is tilted, so different parts get more direct sunlight at different times of year. That tilt is what gives us summer, winter, spring, and fall.

question_text: What mostly causes the ocean tides on Earth?
explanation: The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans, making the water bulge slightly. As the Earth turns, that bulge gives us high and low tides.

question_text: What do we call the shape of the Moon when we cannot see it lit up at all?
explanation: A new moon is when the lit side of the Moon faces away from us, so it looks dark. A few nights later, a thin crescent appears.

question_text: What do we call the Moon when its whole face looks lit up?
explanation: A full moon happens when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, so we see the Moon's whole sunlit side. It is the brightest phase.

question_text: About how long does the Earth take to travel once around the Sun?
explanation: The Earth takes about 365 days to circle the Sun, which is why a year is that long. Every four years, we add a leap day to catch up.

question_text: Where does moonlight actually come from?
options: The Moon glows on its own
explanation: The Moon does not make its own light. It works like a giant mirror, bouncing the Sun's light back to us.

question_text: What is the Sun?
explanation: The Sun is a star, just like the tiny twinkly ones you see at night. It only looks bigger because it is much closer to us.

question_text: What is the Sun mostly made of?
explanation: The Sun is a giant ball of hot gases, mostly hydrogen and helium. Deep inside, hydrogen squishes together and releases the energy that warms us.

question_text: About how long does sunlight take to reach the Earth?
explanation: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to the Earth. So the sunshine you feel is already 8 minutes old by the time it gets here.

question_text: What is the stream of tiny particles flowing out from the Sun called?
explanation: The Sun sends out a steady stream of tiny particles called the solar wind. When it bumps into Earth's atmosphere near the poles, it can create the colorful auroras.

question_text: Why should you never look straight at the Sun?
options: It will turn your eyes yellow
It is too far to see
explanation: The Sun is so bright that staring at it can damage your eyes very quickly. People use special safe glasses to look at it during eclipses.

question_text: What is the name of the galaxy we live in?
explanation: Our galaxy is called the Milky Way. On a very dark night you can see it as a misty band of stars stretching across the sky.

question_text: What is a galaxy?
options: A huge group of stars, gas, and dust
explanation: A galaxy is a giant family of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Our Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars.

question_text: Which star sits almost directly above the North Pole and barely moves in our sky?
explanation: Polaris is also called the North Star. Sailors and travelers used it for hundreds of years to find their way north at night.

question_text: Which famous star pattern looks like a hunter with a belt of three bright stars?
explanation: The constellation Orion is named after a hunter from old stories. The three bright stars in a row make up his belt.

question_text: The Big Dipper is part of a larger constellation that looks like what animal?
explanation: The Big Dipper is part of Ursa Major, which means 'Great Bear' in Latin. The dipper shape forms the bear's back and tail.

question_text: What is a constellation?
options: A pattern of stars in the sky
explanation: A constellation is a group of stars that people imagine forming a picture or shape. Different cultures have invented their own constellations for thousands of years.

question_text: What is the closest big galaxy to our Milky Way?
explanation: Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy to ours. It is so far away that the light we see from it left around 2.5 million years ago.

question_text: What does a 'light-year' measure?
options: How long a year is on the Sun
A distance that light travels in one year
explanation: A light-year is a distance, not a time. It is how far light can travel in one whole year, and light moves incredibly fast.

question_text: What are asteroids?
options: Rocky objects that orbit the Sun
explanation: Asteroids are chunks of rock and metal that orbit the Sun. Most of them live in a band between Mars and Jupiter called the asteroid belt.

question_text: What is the bright tail of a comet mostly made of?
explanation: When a comet gets near the Sun, its ice melts and releases gas and dust. The Sun's light pushes that material into a long, glowing tail.

question_text: What do we call a 'shooting star' streaking across the night sky?
explanation: A 'shooting star' is really a meteor, which is a small piece of rock burning up in our atmosphere. It only looks like a star because it glows so brightly.

question_text: What do we call a space rock that survives its fall and lands on the ground?
explanation: A meteorite is the leftover rock that makes it all the way to the ground. Scientists love to study them because they came from far out in space.

question_text: Pluto used to be called a planet. What is it called now?
explanation: Scientists changed Pluto's title to 'dwarf planet' in 2006 because it is small and shares its orbit area with other icy objects. It is still a fascinating world.

question_text: What was Sputnik 1, launched in 1957?
options: The first rocket to the Moon
The first satellite to orbit the Earth
explanation: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite ever to orbit the Earth. It was launched by the Soviet Union and was about the size of a beach ball.

question_text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
explanation: Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the Moon, in 1969. He famously said it was 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'.

question_text: Which mission carried the first humans to land on the Moon?
explanation: Apollo 11 carried the first astronauts to land on the Moon in July 1969. Two of them walked on the surface while a third orbited above.

question_text: What is the International Space Station?
options: A laboratory orbiting Earth where astronauts live and work
A new planet in our solar system
explanation: The International Space Station is a giant lab that orbits the Earth. Astronauts from many countries live there for months at a time doing experiments.

question_text: What kind of vehicle have scientists sent to drive around on Mars?
explanation: A rover is a robot car that drives across another world. Mars rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance take photos and study the rocks and soil.

question_text: What is the Hubble Space Telescope?
options: A telescope orbiting Earth that takes pictures of space
explanation: Hubble is a telescope that orbits high above the Earth's atmosphere. From up there it can take amazingly clear photos of stars and galaxies.

question_text: The James Webb Space Telescope mostly looks at the universe using what kind of light?
explanation: The James Webb Space Telescope uses infrared light, a kind of light our eyes cannot see. That helps it spot very faint and very distant objects.

question_text: What do we call a person who travels into space?
explanation: People who travel into space are called astronauts, which means 'star sailor'. In Russia they are called cosmonauts.

question_text: Why do astronauts float around inside the Space Station?
options: There is no gravity at all in space
They are constantly falling around the Earth
explanation: The Space Station and the astronauts inside are always falling toward the Earth, but moving sideways so fast they keep missing it. That endless falling makes them feel weightless.

question_text: Which planet has the most moons that we know of?
explanation: Saturn has more known moons than any other planet, with over 140 discovered so far. Its biggest moon, Titan, even has lakes of liquid methane.

question_text: What is the very center of the Earth called?
explanation: The inner core is a hot ball of solid metal at the middle of the Earth. It is mostly made of iron and nickel.

question_text: Which layer of the Earth do we live on top of?
explanation: The crust is the thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth. All the land and ocean floors sit on top of it.

question_text: How many continents are there on Earth?
explanation: Earth has 7 continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

question_text: What is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth called?
explanation: The equator splits the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is the warmest part of the planet because the Sun shines most directly there.

question_text: What are the giant pieces of Earth's crust that slowly move around called?
explanation: Tectonic plates fit together like puzzle pieces. When they bump or slide, they can cause earthquakes and build mountains.

question_text: The North Pole and South Pole are the coldest places on Earth because they get the least what?
explanation: Sunlight hits the poles at a slanted angle, so the warmth spreads out and feels weaker. That is why the poles stay icy all year.

question_text: Which layer of the Earth sits just below the crust?
explanation: The mantle is a thick layer of hot, slow-moving rock. Heat from the mantle is what makes the tectonic plates above it shift.

question_text: If you live north of the equator, which hemisphere are you in?
explanation: The equator divides Earth into two halves called hemispheres. Everything above the equator is in the Northern Hemisphere.

question_text: What is the tallest mountain on Earth above sea level?
explanation: Mount Everest stands about 8,849 meters tall in the Himalayas. It still grows a tiny bit taller each year as the plates push it up.

question_text: How do most mountains form?
explanation: When two plates collide, the land between them crumples and folds upward over millions of years. That slow folding builds mountain ranges.

question_text: What is the hot, melted rock that comes out of a volcano called?
explanation: When melted rock is still underground, it is called magma. Once it reaches the surface, it gets a new name: lava.

question_text: What is an earthquake?
options: A type of wave in the ocean
explanation: Earthquakes happen when tectonic plates suddenly slip past each other underground. The energy travels through the ground and makes it shake.

question_text: The Ring of Fire is a famous area around which ocean?
explanation: The Ring of Fire is a giant horseshoe shape around the Pacific Ocean. Many of the world's volcanoes and earthquakes happen along it.

question_text: What do we call a scientist who studies rocks and the Earth?
explanation: A geologist studies how the Earth is made and how it changes. They look at rocks, fossils, and even volcanoes for clues.

question_text: Which type of rock is formed when lava or magma cools and hardens?
explanation: Igneous rocks come from cooled melted rock. The word igneous comes from a Latin word meaning fire.

question_text: Sandstone and limestone are examples of which kind of rock?
explanation: Sedimentary rocks form when bits of sand, mud, or shells press together over a long time. They often have layers you can see.

question_text: What is a fossil?
options: The preserved remains or trace of an ancient living thing
explanation: Fossils are clues left behind in rock by plants and animals that lived long ago. Dinosaur bones found in stone are famous fossils.

question_text: Which of these is a mineral often used in pencils?
explanation: The dark line a pencil makes on paper is graphite, not lead. Graphite is a soft mineral made of carbon.

question_text: What kind of rock forms when other rocks are changed by heat and pressure deep underground?
explanation: Metamorphic rocks start as another type of rock and slowly transform. For example, limestone can change into marble.

question_text: When water turns into a gas and rises into the air, what is that called?
explanation: Heat from the Sun gives water energy and turns it into invisible water vapor. This is the first step of the water cycle.

question_text: What is it called when water vapor in the air cools and turns back into tiny droplets?
explanation: Condensation is how clouds form, and it is also why a cold glass gets wet on the outside on a warm day.

question_text: Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are all forms of what?
explanation: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds back to the ground. The form it takes depends on how cold the air is.

question_text: Which type of cloud is tall, fluffy, and often brings thunderstorms?
explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds can grow many kilometers tall. They hold lots of water and energy, which is why they cause storms.

question_text: Thin, wispy clouds high up in the sky are called what?
explanation: Cirrus clouds form very high in the sky where the air is freezing. They are made of tiny ice crystals, not water droplets.

question_text: A flat, gray cloud that covers the whole sky like a blanket is called what?
explanation: Stratus clouds form in low, even layers. They often bring drizzle or a gloomy gray day.

question_text: What is hail?
options: Frozen rain that falls as small balls of ice
explanation: Hail forms in tall storm clouds where strong winds toss raindrops up into freezing air over and over. Each trip adds a new layer of ice.

question_text: What is sleet?
options: Tiny pieces of ice from a hailstorm
A mix of rain and snow that freezes as it falls
explanation: Sleet starts as snow, melts into rain, and then freezes again before reaching the ground. It usually feels like little ice pellets.

question_text: Why do we see lightning before we hear thunder?
options: Thunder happens after the storm ends
explanation: Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment, but light reaches our eyes almost instantly while sound takes longer to travel through the air.

question_text: What causes thunder?
options: Air heated very quickly by lightning
explanation: A lightning bolt heats the air around it so fast that the air explodes outward. That sudden burst of air is the rumble we call thunder.

question_text: What two things do you need in the sky to see a rainbow?
explanation: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through tiny water droplets and bends. The light splits into all its colors, making the arch we see.

question_text: What is a tornado?
options: A spinning column of air that reaches from a cloud to the ground
A kind of dust cloud in the desert
explanation: Tornadoes form during powerful thunderstorms when warm and cool air spin together. They can pick up dust and look dark and funnel-shaped.

question_text: Where do hurricanes form?
explanation: Hurricanes need warm seawater to grow. The heat and moisture from the ocean give the storm its power.

question_text: What is fog?
options: A cloud that forms close to the ground
explanation: Fog is just a cloud that forms near the ground when the air cools enough for water vapor to turn into tiny droplets you can walk through.

question_text: What do we call a person who studies and predicts the weather?
explanation: Meteorologists use tools like radar, satellites, and weather stations to figure out what the weather will do next.

question_text: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe?
explanation: About 78% of the air around us is nitrogen. Oxygen is the second most common gas at about 21%.

question_text: Which layer of the atmosphere do we live in, where almost all weather happens?
explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere. Clouds, rain, and wind all happen here, close to the ground.

question_text: What does the ozone layer do for us?
options: It blocks harmful rays from the Sun
explanation: The ozone layer sits high up in the stratosphere. It soaks up most of the Sun's ultraviolet rays so they don't reach the ground.

question_text: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: When greenhouses grow more plants in winter
When some gases in the air trap heat near the Earth
explanation: Certain gases in the atmosphere act like a blanket and hold in warmth. A little bit keeps Earth comfy, but too much can make it warmer than usual.

question_text: Which gas do humans and animals breathe in to stay alive?
explanation: We breathe in oxygen, and our bodies use it to get energy from food. Plants help us by making more oxygen.

question_text: About how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
explanation: Roughly 71% of the Earth is covered by oceans, seas, lakes, and rivers. That is why Earth looks so blue from space.

question_text: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
explanation: The Pacific Ocean is so big it covers more area than all of Earth's land put together. It sits between Asia and the Americas.

question_text: How many oceans are there on Earth?
explanation: There are 5 oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern. They are all connected as one big body of water.

question_text: What makes ocean water taste salty?
options: Salt washed in from rocks and rivers over a long time
explanation: Rain and rivers slowly dissolve tiny bits of salt from rocks on land and carry them to the sea. The salt builds up in the ocean over millions of years.

question_text: What mostly causes the ocean's tides to rise and fall?
options: The pull of the Moon's gravity
explanation: The Moon's gravity tugs on the Earth's water, making it bulge slightly. As Earth turns, this creates the daily rhythm of high and low tides.

question_text: What is the deepest known place in the ocean called?
explanation: The Mariana Trench is in the Pacific Ocean and goes down nearly 11 kilometers. That is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.

question_text: What are the large rivers of moving water inside the ocean called?
explanation: Ocean currents move warm and cold water around the planet. They help shape the weather and even guide many sea animals on their journeys.

question_text: Why does Earth have seasons?
options: Because Earth gets closer and farther from the Sun
Because Earth is tilted on its axis
Because the Sun changes its temperature
explanation: Earth is tilted at about 23.5 degrees. As it orbits the Sun, different parts of the planet lean toward or away from the Sun, which gives us the seasons.

question_text: When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, what season is it in the Southern Hemisphere?
explanation: The two hemispheres are tilted in opposite directions, so they have opposite seasons. When the north is warm, the south is cool.

question_text: What is a solstice?
options: A day when day and night are about the same length
The longest or shortest day of the year
The first day of spring rain
A day when the Moon is full
explanation: A solstice happens twice a year. One brings the longest day of the year, and the other brings the shortest, depending on which hemisphere you live in.

question_text: Why do places near the North and South Poles have days that last for months?
options: Because the Sun grows brighter there
Because Earth's tilt points them toward the Sun for a long time
explanation: When a pole is tilted toward the Sun, it stays in sunlight all day long for many weeks. Six months later, that same pole is tilted away and stays dark instead.

question_text: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
explanation: Roots grow down into the soil and soak up water and minerals that the plant needs to grow.

question_text: What do plants use to make their own food?
explanation: Plants use sunlight, water, and a gas in the air called carbon dioxide to make their own food in a process called photosynthesis.

question_text: What gas do plants give off that humans need to breathe?
explanation: When plants make food using sunlight, they release oxygen into the air. That is the same oxygen we breathe in.

question_text: What is the job of a flower on a plant?
explanation: Flowers help plants make seeds. After a flower is pollinated, it can grow into a fruit that holds new seeds.

question_text: How do bees help flowers?
explanation: Bees pick up tiny grains of pollen on their fuzzy bodies and carry it from flower to flower, helping plants make seeds.

question_text: What is it called when a seed starts to grow into a new plant?
explanation: Germination is when a seed wakes up and starts to sprout. Most seeds need water and warmth to germinate.

question_text: Which of these is one way seeds can travel away from a plant?
explanation: Some seeds, like dandelion fluff or maple keys, are shaped to ride the wind to a new spot where they can grow.

question_text: What do we call trees that lose their leaves every autumn?
explanation: Deciduous trees, like oaks and maples, drop their leaves each fall to save energy through the cold winter.

question_text: Which part of the plant carries water from the roots up to the leaves?
explanation: The stem works like a straw, carrying water and nutrients from the roots up to the leaves and flowers.

question_text: Why do leaves look green?
options: Because of a green substance called chlorophyll
explanation: Leaves contain chlorophyll, a green substance that captures sunlight and helps the plant make food.

question_text: How can you tell how old a tree is by looking at a cut stump?
explanation: Each year a tree grows a new ring of wood. By counting the rings, you can find out how many years the tree has been alive.

question_text: Even though we eat it like a vegetable, a tomato is actually a what?
explanation: In science, a fruit is the part of a plant that holds seeds. Tomatoes have seeds inside, so they are technically fruits.

question_text: When you eat a carrot, which part of the plant are you eating?
explanation: Carrots are roots that grow underground and store food for the plant. That stored food makes them sweet and crunchy.

question_text: What are the tiny building blocks that make up all living things?
explanation: Cells are the smallest units of life. Your body, plants, and even tiny germs are all made of cells.

question_text: What does a plant cell have that an animal cell does not?
explanation: Plant cells have a tough cell wall around them that helps the plant stand up straight. Animal cells do not have this wall.

question_text: An amoeba is a tiny creature made of how many cells?
explanation: An amoeba is a single-celled organism. Its whole body is just one cell, and you usually need a microscope to see it.

question_text: In a food chain, what do we call plants that make their own food?
explanation: Plants are called producers because they produce, or make, their own food using sunlight. They start most food chains.

question_text: What do we call living things that eat other living things for energy?
explanation: Consumers cannot make their own food, so they consume, or eat, plants and other animals to get the energy they need.

question_text: Mushrooms and many bacteria break down dead plants and animals. What are these helpers called?
explanation: Decomposers break down dead things and return their nutrients to the soil, so new plants can grow with that food.

question_text: Where does the energy in almost every food chain originally come from?
explanation: The Sun gives energy to plants, plants are eaten by animals, and so on. Almost all energy in food chains starts with the Sun.

question_text: In a predator and prey pair, which one gets eaten?
explanation: The prey is the animal that gets hunted and eaten. The predator is the one doing the hunting.

question_text: Which biome is hot, very dry, and gets little rain?
explanation: Deserts are very dry places that get less than 10 inches of rain a year. Plants and animals there are built to save water.

question_text: Which biome has tall trees, lots of rain, and many kinds of plants and animals?
explanation: Rainforests get rain almost every day. They are warm and packed with more types of plants and animals than anywhere else on Earth.

question_text: The tundra is a biome that is mostly what?
explanation: The tundra is one of the coldest places on Earth. The ground stays frozen most of the year, so trees cannot grow there.

question_text: A pond, river, or lake is part of which kind of ecosystem?
explanation: Freshwater ecosystems have water without much salt. Many fish, frogs, and insects live in freshwater ponds, rivers, and lakes.

question_text: What is the second stage in a butterfly's life cycle, after the egg?
explanation: After hatching from an egg, a butterfly is a caterpillar. It eats lots of leaves before turning into a chrysalis.

question_text: What do baby frogs that have just hatched from eggs look like?
explanation: Baby frogs are called tadpoles. They have tails and live in water, then slowly grow legs and lose their tails as they become frogs.

question_text: What is the very first stage in the life cycle of most flowering plants?
explanation: A new plant starts as a seed. With water, warmth, and soil, the seed germinates and grows into a sprout, then a full plant.

question_text: About how many bones are in a fully grown adult human body?
explanation: Adults have about 206 bones. Together they form the skeleton, which holds your body up and protects your insides.

question_text: Babies are actually born with more bones than adults. Why do adults have fewer?
options: Some bones fuse together as you grow
explanation: Babies have around 270 bones. As they grow up, some small bones join, or fuse, together to make bigger ones, leaving about 206.

question_text: What is the longest bone in the human body?
explanation: The femur is the thigh bone that runs from your hip to your knee. It is the longest and one of the strongest bones you have.

question_text: Where is the smallest bone in your body found?
explanation: The stapes, found inside your ear, is the smallest bone in your body. It helps pass sound vibrations so you can hear.

question_text: What is the main job of your heart?
options: To pump blood around your body
explanation: Your heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood through your body. The blood carries oxygen and nutrients to every part of you.

question_text: What is the main job of your lungs?
explanation: Your lungs help you breathe. They pull in oxygen from the air and push out a gas called carbon dioxide that your body does not need.

question_text: When you breathe in, which gas does your body take from the air?
explanation: We breathe in oxygen because every cell in our body needs it to work. We then breathe out carbon dioxide.

question_text: What is your pulse?
options: The beat of your heart you can feel
explanation: Each time your heart beats, it pushes blood through your body. You can feel that push as a pulse on your wrist or neck.

question_text: About how many senses do humans usually use to learn about the world?
explanation: We usually talk about five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Each one uses a different part of your body.

question_text: Which body part lets in light so you can see?
explanation: The pupil is the black circle in the middle of your eye. It opens wider in the dark and gets smaller in bright light.

question_text: What is the colored ring around the pupil of your eye called?
explanation: The iris is the colored part of your eye. It can be brown, blue, green, or hazel, and it controls how much light goes into the pupil.

question_text: What is the name of the thin part inside your ear that vibrates when sound hits it?
explanation: Your eardrum is a thin layer that vibrates when sound waves reach it. Those vibrations help your brain understand sounds.

question_text: Which body part do you mostly use to taste your food?
explanation: Your tongue is covered in tiny taste buds that pick up flavors like sweet, salty, sour, and bitter.

question_text: How many teeth does a typical adult have?
explanation: Adults usually have 32 teeth, including wisdom teeth at the back. Each kind of tooth has a different job in chewing.

question_text: How many baby teeth does a child usually grow before adult teeth come in?
explanation: Children usually have 20 baby teeth. They start falling out around age 6 and are slowly replaced by 32 adult teeth.

question_text: Which kind of teeth are flat and wide for grinding food?
explanation: Molars are the big, flat teeth at the back of your mouth. They grind and crush food so it is easier to swallow.

question_text: Which organ controls everything you think, feel, and do?
explanation: Your brain is the control center of your body. It sends messages through nerves to tell every part what to do.

question_text: If a doctor taps your knee and your leg jumps without you trying, what is that called?
explanation: A reflex is a fast, automatic move your body makes without you having to think about it. It helps protect you from harm.

question_text: Where does most of your food go to be broken down after you swallow it?
explanation: Food goes from your mouth to your stomach, where it is mashed up, and then into your intestines, where the goodness is taken in.

question_text: Eating fruits and vegetables is a great way to get what important nutrients?
explanation: Fruits and vegetables are full of vitamins and minerals that help your body grow strong and stay healthy.

question_text: What do muscles do to help your body move?
explanation: Muscles are attached to your bones. When a muscle tightens, it pulls a bone, and that is how you move your arms, legs, and face.

question_text: What is the largest organ of the human body?
explanation: Your skin is your biggest organ. It covers your whole body, protects your insides, and helps keep you the right temperature.

question_text: What are the three main states of matter?
explanation: Matter usually comes in three forms: solid (like ice), liquid (like water), and gas (like steam). Plasma is sometimes called a fourth state.

question_text: At what temperature does water freeze?
explanation: Water freezes into ice at 32°F, which is 0°C. Below that temperature, the water molecules slow down and lock into a solid shape.

question_text: At what temperature does water boil?
explanation: Water boils at 212°F, or 100°C, turning into a gas called water vapor. That's why a kettle whistles when the steam rushes out.

question_text: What is it called when a liquid turns into a gas?
explanation: Evaporation is when a liquid turns into a gas, like a puddle drying up in the sun. The water becomes invisible water vapor in the air.

question_text: What is it called when a gas turns back into a liquid?
explanation: Condensation happens when water vapor in the air cools down and turns into tiny drops of liquid. That's why a cold glass gets wet on the outside.

question_text: What are the tiny building blocks that everything is made of?
explanation: Atoms are incredibly tiny pieces that make up everything around us, from your toes to the stars. You'd need millions just to make a speck of dust.

question_text: What does the chemical formula H2O stand for?
explanation: H2O is water. It means each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom joined together.

question_text: Which gas do we breathe out that plants like to use?
explanation: We breathe out carbon dioxide, written as CO2. Plants take in CO2 to help them make food and grow.

question_text: If you took a rock to the Moon, what would change?
options: Its weight would change but its mass would stay the same
Both its mass and weight would change
Its mass would change but its weight would stay the same
explanation: Mass is how much stuff something is made of, and that doesn't change. Weight depends on gravity, and the Moon has weaker gravity than Earth.

question_text: What is it called when a solid turns straight into a gas, skipping liquid?
explanation: Sublimation is when a solid turns directly into a gas. Dry ice does this, which is why it makes spooky fog without leaving a puddle.

question_text: What force pulls things down toward the ground?
explanation: Gravity is the force that pulls everything toward the center of the Earth. It's also what keeps the planets moving around the Sun.

question_text: What force makes a sliding ball slow down and stop?
explanation: Friction happens when two surfaces rub together, slowing things down and creating a little heat. Try rubbing your hands together fast!

question_text: What happens when you put the north poles of two magnets together?
options: They turn into one big magnet
explanation: Like poles repel each other, so two north poles push apart. Opposite poles, like north and south, snap together.

question_text: Which metal is strongly attracted to magnets?
explanation: Iron is one of the few metals that magnets pull on. Most coins, gold, and aluminum foil don't stick to magnets at all.

question_text: What are the two basic kinds of forces?
explanation: Every force is either a push or a pull. Kicking a ball is a push, and pulling a wagon is a pull.

question_text: An object that is sitting still will keep sitting still unless what?
options: A force pushes or pulls it
explanation: This is called inertia. A still object won't move on its own; something has to push or pull it to get it going.

question_text: Which of these is a simple machine?
explanation: A lever is a simple machine, like a seesaw or a crowbar. Simple machines have few or no moving parts but make work easier.

question_text: A ramp is an example of which simple machine?
explanation: A ramp is an inclined plane. It makes it easier to move heavy things up to a higher place by spreading the work over a longer distance.

question_text: What kind of simple machine is a flagpole rope used to raise a flag?
explanation: A pulley uses a wheel and a rope to lift things more easily. Pulling down on one end makes the other end go up.

question_text: What kind of energy does a moving bicycle have?
explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Anything that's moving, like a runner or a rolling ball, has kinetic energy.

question_text: What kind of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band?
explanation: Potential energy is stored energy waiting to be used. When you let the rubber band go, that stored energy becomes motion.

question_text: What kind of energy does a battery store?
explanation: Batteries hold chemical energy inside them. When a battery is in a circuit, that chemical energy turns into electricity.

question_text: Which of these is a renewable energy source?
explanation: Sunlight is renewable because it keeps coming every day. Coal, oil, and gas are nonrenewable, meaning once we use them up, they're gone.

question_text: Which of these uses moving air to make electricity?
explanation: Wind turbines have giant blades that spin when the wind blows, and that spinning motion gets turned into electricity.

question_text: When you turn on a lamp, electrical energy mostly turns into what?
explanation: A light bulb changes electricity into light energy, and a little bit becomes heat. That's why a bulb feels warm after it's been on.

question_text: How does light travel?
explanation: Light travels in straight lines until it hits something. That's why shadows are sharp and flashlights make a clear beam.

question_text: About how fast does light travel?
explanation: Light zooms at about 186,000 miles every single second. Nothing in the universe travels faster than light.

question_text: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth from the Sun?
explanation: Sunlight travels for about 8 minutes before it gets to Earth. So the sunshine you feel right now actually left the Sun 8 minutes ago.

question_text: What is it called when light bounces off a surface like a mirror?
explanation: Reflection is when light bounces off something. A mirror is so smooth that it reflects light perfectly, showing you your face.

question_text: What happens when sunlight passes through a glass prism?
explanation: A prism bends light and splits it into the colors of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

question_text: What are the three primary colors of light?
explanation: The primary colors of light are red, green, and blue. When all three mix together, they make white light. This is different from paint colors!

question_text: What makes a shadow?
explanation: A shadow forms when something blocks the light. Since light travels in straight lines, it can't bend around the object to fill the dark space behind it.

question_text: Why does the sky look blue during the day?
options: The ocean reflects up onto the sky
Blue light scatters more in the air
explanation: Sunlight has all the colors, but blue light bounces around in the air more than the others. That scattered blue light fills the sky.

question_text: What is sound made of?
explanation: Sound is made of vibrations that travel through air, water, or other materials. When the vibrations reach your ear, your brain hears them as sound.

question_text: Where can sound NOT travel?
explanation: Outer space is empty, with no air or matter for vibrations to move through. That's why space is silent, no matter how big the explosion.

question_text: What do you call sound that bounces back to you off a wall or cliff?
explanation: An echo is sound bouncing off a hard surface and coming back to your ears. Bats and dolphins use echoes to find their way around.

question_text: What do we call how high or low a sound is?
explanation: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. A tiny bird's tweet has a high pitch, and a big drum has a low pitch.

question_text: Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?
options: Light travels much faster than sound
explanation: Light is way faster than sound, so the flash reaches you almost instantly while the boom takes longer to arrive. The closer the storm, the smaller the gap.

question_text: What word describes how loud or quiet a sound is?
explanation: Volume is how loud or quiet a sound is. Turning up the volume on a TV makes the sound louder, not higher.

question_text: Which of these materials is the best conductor of electricity?
explanation: Copper is a metal, and metals let electricity flow through them easily. That's why most electrical wires have copper inside.

question_text: Which of these is an insulator that blocks electricity?
explanation: Rubber is an insulator, meaning electricity can't easily move through it. That's why electrical wires are wrapped in rubber or plastic to keep us safe.

question_text: Why does a balloon stick to your hair after you rub it?
explanation: Rubbing the balloon moves tiny particles called electrons around, creating static electricity. The balloon and your hair then pull toward each other.

question_text: What does an electric circuit need to work?
explanation: Electricity has to flow in a complete loop. If the loop is broken anywhere, the electricity stops and the device turns off.

question_text: What is lightning?
explanation: Lightning is a huge spark of electricity that jumps between clouds or from a cloud to the ground. It can be hotter than the surface of the Sun.

question_text: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
explanation: Gold's symbol is Au, from its old Latin name 'aurum,' which means 'shining dawn.' Each element has its own short symbol.

question_text: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen, the gas we breathe in?
explanation: Oxygen's symbol is just the letter O. Our lungs pull oxygen out of the air every time we take a breath.

question_text: Which of these is an acid?
explanation: Lemon juice is acidic, which is why it tastes so sour. Soap and baking soda are bases, the opposite of acids.

question_text: What is table salt's chemical name?
explanation: Table salt is sodium chloride, written as NaCl. It's made of one sodium atom joined with one chlorine atom.

question_text: Which of these is a solution, where one thing dissolves into another?
explanation: When salt is stirred into water, it disappears into the liquid, making a solution. Sand just sinks and stays separate, so it's only a mixture.

question_text: What three things does a fire need to burn?
explanation: This is called the fire triangle: fuel (something to burn), oxygen (from the air), and heat. Take any one away and the fire goes out.

question_text: Which scientist is famous for figuring out how gravity works after watching an apple fall?
explanation: Isaac Newton wondered why apples fall down instead of up, which led him to describe gravity, the force that pulls things toward each other.

question_text: Albert Einstein is best known for his theory of what?
explanation: Einstein's theory of relativity changed how we think about time, space, and energy. His famous equation E=mc squared came from this work.

question_text: Galileo Galilei used which instrument to study the Moon and planets?
explanation: Galileo improved the telescope and pointed it at the sky. He saw mountains on the Moon and four moons orbiting Jupiter.

question_text: Nicolaus Copernicus suggested that what is at the center of our solar system?
explanation: Long ago, most people thought Earth was the center. Copernicus showed that the Sun is at the center and the planets orbit around it.

question_text: Marie Curie is famous for her research on what?
explanation: Marie Curie discovered radioactive elements like radium and polonium. She was the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes.

question_text: Which scientist developed the theory of evolution after visiting the Galapagos Islands?
explanation: Charles Darwin noticed that finches on different islands had different beaks. This helped him explain how living things change over time.

question_text: Gregor Mendel discovered the basics of genetics by studying which plant?
explanation: Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and tracked traits like flower color. His work showed how parents pass features to their children.

question_text: Louis Pasteur is famous for showing that what causes many diseases?
explanation: Pasteur proved that tiny living germs can make people sick. He also invented pasteurization, which heats milk to kill harmful germs.

question_text: Alexander Fleming discovered which life-saving medicine in 1928?
explanation: Fleming noticed mold growing in his lab was killing bacteria. That mold became penicillin, the first antibiotic, which has saved millions of lives.

question_text: Edwin Hubble made an important discovery about what?
explanation: Hubble showed that there are billions of galaxies beyond our Milky Way and that they are moving apart. The famous Hubble Space Telescope is named after him.

question_text: Stephen Hawking was a scientist who studied what mysterious objects in space?
explanation: Stephen Hawking helped us understand black holes, regions in space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

question_text: Rosalind Franklin's photographs helped scientists discover the shape of what?
explanation: Franklin's X-ray pictures showed that DNA, the instruction code in our cells, has a twisted ladder shape called a double helix.

question_text: Jane Goodall spent her life studying which kind of animal?
explanation: Jane Goodall lived in the forests of Tanzania and watched chimpanzees up close. She showed that they use tools, just like people do.

question_text: Katherine Johnson was a brilliant mathematician who worked for which organization?
explanation: Katherine Johnson did the math that helped NASA send astronauts safely into space and back. Her calculations were checked by hand before computers were trusted.

question_text: Thomas Edison is most famous for inventing a practical version of what?
explanation: Edison tested thousands of materials before finding one that made a long-lasting light bulb. He also invented the phonograph, which could record sound.

question_text: Nikola Tesla helped develop which kind of electricity that powers most homes today?
explanation: Tesla designed systems for alternating current, or AC, which can travel long distances through wires. That is the kind of electricity in your wall outlets.

question_text: Alexander Graham Bell is credited with inventing what?
explanation: Bell invented the telephone in 1876. His first words spoken on it were to his assistant in another room.

question_text: The Wright Brothers made history in 1903 by being the first to do what?
explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright flew the first powered airplane at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The flight only lasted 12 seconds but changed the world.

question_text: Johannes Gutenberg invented a machine that made it easier to print what?
explanation: Gutenberg's printing press from the 1440s could make many copies of books quickly. Before that, books had to be copied by hand and very few people had them.

question_text: Tim Berners-Lee is famous for inventing what in 1989?
explanation: Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web, which lets people share pages and links across the internet. He gave it away for free so anyone could use it.

question_text: Henry Ford changed how cars were built by using what?
explanation: Ford's assembly line had each worker add just one part as the car moved past. This made cars cheap enough for regular families to own.

question_text: Garrett Morgan invented an early version of which safety device used on roads?
explanation: Morgan invented a three-position traffic signal in 1923 that helped cars take turns safely at busy intersections. He also invented an early gas mask.

question_text: Hedy Lamarr was a movie star who also helped invent technology used in what?
explanation: Lamarr co-invented a frequency-hopping system during World War II. The same idea helps modern Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GPS work today.

question_text: Granville Woods invented a system that let trains do what?
explanation: Woods created a way for moving trains to send messages to stations using telegraph signals. This made train travel much safer by preventing crashes.

question_text: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak started which famous technology company?
explanation: Jobs and Wozniak built their first Apple computer in a garage in California in 1976. Apple later made the iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

question_text: Velcro was invented after a man noticed what stuck to his dog's fur?
explanation: Swiss inventor George de Mestral saw burrs sticking to his dog and looked at them under a microscope. He copied the tiny hooks to make Velcro.

question_text: Post-it notes were invented when a scientist accidentally created what?
options: Glue that was only a little sticky
explanation: A 3M scientist tried to make super-strong glue but ended up with a weak one that peeled off easily. That gentle stickiness was perfect for sticky notes.

question_text: The microwave oven was discovered when an engineer noticed what melted in his pocket?
explanation: Percy Spencer was working near a radar machine when the chocolate in his pocket melted. He realized the waves were heating food and invented the microwave.

question_text: Inside a computer, which part acts like the brain and does the thinking?
explanation: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit. It carries out the instructions that make programs and games work.

question_text: Which part of a computer stores files even when the power is off?
explanation: The hard drive is long-term memory that keeps your photos, games, and documents safe when the computer is shut down.

question_text: Computers do all their work using only two numbers. What are they?
explanation: This is called binary. Inside a computer, a 1 means a switch is on and a 0 means it is off. Long strings of 1s and 0s make everything work.

question_text: GPS, which helps maps know where you are, works using what?
explanation: GPS stands for Global Positioning System. Your phone listens to signals from satellites circling Earth to figure out exactly where you are.

question_text: What does it mean to write code or program a computer?
options: Giving the computer instructions to follow
explanation: Programming means writing step-by-step instructions in a special language the computer understands. Scratch and Python are languages kids often start with.

question_text: The first computers built in the 1940s were about the size of what?
explanation: Early computers like ENIAC filled entire rooms and weighed many tons. Today a phone in your pocket is millions of times more powerful.

question_text: What is a robot?
options: A machine that can be programmed to do tasks
explanation: A robot is a machine that follows instructions to do jobs by itself. Some robots build cars, some explore Mars, and some even vacuum floors.

question_text: What does AI stand for?
explanation: Artificial intelligence means computer programs that can learn and solve problems in ways that seem smart. Voice assistants and chatbots use AI.

question_text: A modern smartphone replaces many older devices. Which of these is NOT one of them?
explanation: Phones have absorbed cameras, calculators, maps, music players, flashlights, and more. But they still cannot keep your food cold.

question_text: What is the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web?
options: The internet is the network of computers; the Web is the pages and links on it
They are exactly the same thing
The Web is older than the internet
The internet only works on phones
explanation: The internet is the giant network connecting computers. The Web is one thing you can use on the internet, made of pages you visit in a browser.

question_text: In science, what is a hypothesis?
options: A smart guess that you test with an experiment
explanation: A hypothesis is your best guess about what will happen. Scientists test it with experiments to see if the guess turns out to be right or wrong.

question_text: Which tool would you use to look at something tiny like a single cell?
explanation: A microscope uses lenses to make very small things look much bigger. Scientists use them to study cells, bacteria, and other tiny objects.

question_text: What do doctors use a stethoscope for?
explanation: A stethoscope makes the quiet sounds inside your body louder. Doctors press it to your chest to hear your heart beating and your lungs breathing.

question_text: Which instrument measures how hot or cold something is?
explanation: A thermometer measures temperature. Some show numbers on a screen, while older ones use a thin line of liquid that rises when it gets warmer.

question_text: When scientists run an experiment, what is a variable?
options: The room where work is done
Something you change or measure in the test
explanation: A variable is anything that can change in an experiment, like the amount of water you give plants. Scientists usually change just one at a time to see what it does.

question_text: What does it mean to make an observation in science?
options: To use your senses to notice and learn about something
To prove an idea is wrong
To draw a picture from memory
explanation: Observation means carefully watching, listening, smelling, or touching to gather information. Good observations are the start of almost every science discovery.

question_text: How do vaccines help keep us healthy?
options: They cure you after you are already sick
They train the body to fight germs before you get sick
explanation: A vaccine teaches your immune system to recognize a germ. If the real germ shows up later, your body already knows how to fight it off.

question_text: Wilhelm Roentgen discovered a kind of ray that can take pictures of what?
explanation: Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895. They pass through soft skin but not through bones, so X-ray pictures show your skeleton.

question_text: Why is washing your hands with soap such an important habit?
options: It removes germs that could make you sick
explanation: Soap breaks apart the outer layer of many germs and lets water rinse them away. Twenty seconds of scrubbing does the trick.

question_text: Antibiotic medicines are used to fight which kind of germ?
explanation: Antibiotics work against bacterial infections like strep throat. They do not work on viruses, which is why they cannot cure a cold or the flu.

question_text: What is the main job of a bandage on a small cut?
options: To make the cut heal in one minute
To keep the cut clean and protected while it heals
To stop the skin from feeling cold
To change the color of the skin
explanation: Bandages cover a cut so dirt and germs cannot get in. Your body still does the healing underneath, usually in a few days.

question_text: What kind of tool would you use to measure how much something weighs?
explanation: A scale measures weight or mass. Bathroom scales tell people their weight, and kitchen scales help cooks measure ingredients.
